question: Which of these is true of JSON?
answers: It is text that holds objects in curly braces and lists in square brackets
It knows numbers, text, true, false and null
It hands every value over as text, numbers included
It can only be read by JavaScript
explanation: JSON keeps 11.6 a number and true a boolean. Python reads it with json.loads into a dictionary; every browser has a reader built in too.

question: In {"temperature": 11.6, "unit": "°C"}, read into reading, what is right?
answers: temperature and unit are keys, 11.6 and "°C" their values
reading["temperature"] gives 11.6
reading["Temperature"] also gives 11.6
reading[0] gives 11.6
explanation: You pick a value by its key, letter for letter. A capital T gives a KeyError, and a dictionary has no positions to count.

question: data = {"location": {"lat": 48.2}, "last_three": [11.6, 12.0, 12.4]}. Which lines are right?
answers: data["location"]["lat"] gives 48.2
data["last_three"][0] gives 11.6
data["lat"] gives 48.2
data["last_three"][1] gives 11.6
explanation: Go in step by step: first the outer key, then the inner one. Lists count from 0, so [0] is the first entry.

question: What is an API, like the one the Vienna sensors answer through?
answers: A web address that answers programs with data, usually JSON
Something you ask with an HTTP GET and query parameters such as interval
A web page designed for people to read
A file that must be downloaded and installed first
explanation: An API answers a program, not a person. You can still open its URL in a browser and see the raw JSON.

question: What does R30/2025-10-17T00:00/P1D ask for?
answers: 30 values, one per day, starting 17 October 2025 at midnight
The same 30 days as R60/2025-10-17T00:00/PT12H, cut into days instead of half days
One value for the whole of October 2025
30 values, one per hour
explanation: R is repeat, P is period, T says a time follows: P1D is one day, PT12H twelve hours. Sixty half days are the same thirty days.

question: Which of these is true of XML?
answers: Values sit between an opening and a closing tag, like <temperature>11.6</temperature>
Read with xml.etree, 11.6 comes back as the text '11.6'
It is never used any more
It is always shorter than JSON
explanation: XML hands everything over as text and writes most names twice, in the opening and closing tag. It lives on in gbXML, SVG, KML and inside every .docx file.
